ASHEVILLE, North Carolina (CNN) -- In 1988, a relatively unknown rock and blues guitarist named Warren Haynes got some of his friends together to play music in Asheville, North Carolina. It was just an opportunity for local musicians to jam during the holidays, the one time of year they were all in town together. Warren Haynes' good work has been noted by the street named after him. The artists also wanted to give back to the community, so they gave the money raised by their show to various charities. The tradition has continued. Now celebrating its 20th anniversary, Haynes' Christmas Jam has evolved into an epic annual event for the musicians, fans, and particularly Habitat for Humanity. "We need Habitat For Humanity more now than ever, with the whole mortgage crisis that put us where we are now, and the fact that Habitat is about building homes for people that can't afford homes as opposed to lending money to people who can't afford homes," Haynes told CNN. Haynes and his wife, Stefani Scamardo, decided to donate 100 percent of the Christmas Jam proceeds to Habitat for Humanity years ago because they could see exactly where the money was going. They go back each year and meet the families they helped build homes for. Singer Joan Osborne echoed Haynes' thoughts. "It's a scary time. A lot of people are losing their homes so it's good to be able to do something that helps with that specific problem," she said. Going into 2008's shows, which were held December 12 and 13, the Christmas Jam had raised more than $665,000 for Asheville's Habitat For Humanity. The money has gone into building 12 houses in Enka Hills, a wooded community surrounded by mountains on a street the organization appropriately named Warren Haynes Drive. (In 2005 Habitat also built a house in the New Orleans Musicians Village.) The Thursday before the show, Haynes presented the key to a new home to single mother Suzie Cromer and her 8-year-old daughter. "Meeting the families and seeing the work that Habitat's doing with our help -- you know its hard to see that and not get emotional," Haynes said. "Warren is a hero in our mind," said Habitat's Arianne Kjellquist. "In western North Carolina, the housing costs are really out of whack with what the local wages are, so there's a big discrepancy there. There are more people that maybe would have been approved previously when the lending standards weren't so strict." This year's Christmas Jam lived up to the long-lasting and crowd-pleasing traditions of previous shows. The first night's show ran more than nine hours, ending with an Allman Brothers set after 4 a.m. The second night's show ended at 3:30 a.m. Performers included Ben Harper and Relentless 7, Travis Tritt, Michael Franti, Osborne, Ivan Neville's Dumpstaphunk, Steve Earle and Haynes' band Gov't Mule. Perhaps the most anticipated addition this year among both fans and artists was former Led Zeppelin member John Paul Jones, who played acoustic mandolin, bass and keyboards throughout the weekend with just about everyone. Jones said he was happy to pitch in. "In the economic climate like this, people really just want to get out and enjoy themselves and forget about the day to day stuff that they have to deal with. So it works on many levels," Jones said. "The fact that it is for a good cause is just a huge bonus." Haynes says the 20-year evolution of the Christmas Jam reflects his career. "We've grown up together. Its a parallel of the progress that I have achieved, and the event reflects not only the philosophy I share with these people but the mission." And as fans danced the night away while the artists played their hearts out, families' dreams of owning their perfect home come true. "I would have never imagined or dreamed that it would turn into what its turned into," Haynes reflected with a huge smile.

"We need Habitat For Humanity more now than ever, with the whole mortgage crisis that put us where we are now, and the fact that Habitat is about building homes for people that can't afford homes as opposed to lending money to people who can't afford homes," Haynes explained to CNN.

Some years back, Haynes and his wife, Stefani Scamardo, chose to give every dollar of the Christmas Jam earnings to Habitat for Humanity, largely because they could witness firsthand how the funds were being used. Every year they return to visit the families whose homes they helped make possible.

Singer Joan Osborne shared a similar sentiment. "It's a scary time. A lot of people are losing their homes so it's good to be able to do something that helps with that specific problem," she noted.

By the time the 2008 concerts rolled around on December 12 and 13, the Christmas Jam had generated over $665,000 for Asheville's Habitat For Humanity. Those funds financed the construction of 12 homes in Enka Hills, a tree-filled neighborhood nestled among the mountains, on a road the organization fittingly christened Warren Haynes Drive. (Back in 2005, Habitat had also constructed a home in the New Orleans Musicians Village.)

On the Thursday preceding the concerts, Haynes handed the keys to a brand-new house over to single mother Suzie Cromer and her 8-year-old daughter.

"Meeting the families and seeing the work that Habitat's doing with our help -- you know its hard to see that and not get emotional," Haynes said.

"Warren is a hero in our mind," remarked Habitat's Arianne Kjellquist. "In western North Carolina, the housing costs are really out of whack with what the local wages are, so there's a big discrepancy there. There are more people that maybe would have been approved previously when the lending standards weren't so strict."

The 2008 Christmas Jam honored the enduring, audience-favorite customs established in earlier years. The opening night stretched beyond nine hours, wrapping up with an Allman Brothers performance sometime past 4 a.m., while the following evening concluded at 3:30 a.m. The lineup featured Ben Harper and Relentless 7, Travis Tritt, Michael Franti, Osborne, Ivan Neville's Dumpstaphunk, Steve Earle, and Haynes' own group, Gov't Mule.

Arguably the most eagerly awaited newcomer that year, in the eyes of both fans and fellow musicians, was John Paul Jones, formerly of Led Zeppelin. Throughout the weekend he joined nearly every act, performing on acoustic mandolin, bass, and keyboards.

Jones expressed his gladness at being able to contribute. "In the economic climate like this, people really just want to get out and enjoy themselves and forget about the day to day stuff that they have to deal with. So it works on many levels," Jones said. "The fact that it is for a good cause is just a huge bonus."

According to Haynes, the way the Christmas Jam has developed over 20 years mirrors his own professional journey. "We've grown up together. Its a parallel of the progress that I have achieved, and the event reflects not only the philosophy I share with these people but the mission."

While concertgoers danced through the night and the musicians poured their souls into every song, families saw their hopes of owning an ideal home become reality.

"I would have never imagined or dreamed that it would turn into what its turned into," Haynes said, beaming broadly as he looked back.

What began as a modest gathering of friends and fellow musicians has grown into one of Asheville's most cherished holiday traditions. In 1988, celebrated guitarist Warren Haynes founded the Christmas Jam in his hometown of Asheville, North Carolina, with a simple but heartfelt vision: to bring local musicians together during the holiday season while giving back to the community that had shaped him.

The concept was straightforward yet powerful. Rather than simply celebrating the holidays among peers, Haynes wanted the annual event to serve a greater purpose. By donating the proceeds from the concerts to charity, the Christmas Jam transformed an evening of music into an act of collective generosity. Musicians who might otherwise be scattered across the country during the holidays now had a reason to return home, reconnect with old friends, and share their talents for a worthy cause.

Over the years, the Christmas Jam has flourished into something far greater than its founders could have imagined. Now celebrating its 20th anniversary, the event has become a signature fixture on Asheville's cultural calendar, drawing talented performers and enthusiastic audiences year after year.

The impact of this musical tradition extends well beyond the stage. To date, the Christmas Jam has raised more than $665,000 for Asheville's Habitat for Humanity, a remarkable achievement that has translated directly into brick-and-mortar results. Those funds have enabled the construction of 12 homes for local families in need—families who now have safe, stable places to call their own.

This contribution has proven especially meaningful given the difficult economic climate. Amid the turmoil of the mortgage crisis, when so many families faced housing insecurity and financial hardship, the Christmas Jam's support for Habitat for Humanity offered a genuine lifeline. What Warren Haynes started as a way for musicians to celebrate the holidays together has, two decades later, become a testament to the enduring power of community, compassion, and the belief that music can build more than memories—it can build homes.

# Asheville, North Carolina

Nestled in the heart of the Blue Ridge Mountains, Asheville, North Carolina, is a vibrant city celebrated for its stunning natural beauty, rich cultural scene, and unique mountain charm. As one of the most popular destinations in the southeastern United States, Asheville attracts visitors from around the world who come to experience its distinctive blend of outdoor adventure and artistic sophistication.

## A City Surrounded by Natural Splendor

Located in western North Carolina, Asheville is enveloped by breathtaking mountain landscapes. The nearby Blue Ridge Parkway offers scenic drives with panoramic views, while numerous hiking trails, waterfalls, and forests provide endless opportunities for outdoor enthusiasts. The changing seasons bring spectacular displays of color, making the region particularly popular during the autumn months when the foliage transforms into vivid shades of red, orange, and gold.

## The Iconic Biltmore Estate

No visit to Asheville is complete without exploring the famous Biltmore Estate. Built by George Vanderbilt in the late 19th century, this magnificent mansion is the largest privately owned home in the United States. Visitors can tour its opulent rooms, stroll through beautifully manicured gardens, and enjoy wine tastings at the estate's renowned winery.

## A Thriving Arts and Culinary Scene

Asheville has earned a reputation as a haven for artists, musicians, and creative individuals. The downtown area is filled with galleries, studios, and performance venues. The city is also famous for its craft beer culture, often referred to as "Beer City USA," boasting a remarkable number of breweries per capita.

The local food scene is equally impressive, featuring farm-to-table restaurants that highlight the region's fresh, locally sourced ingredients.

## A Welcoming Community

Beyond its attractions, Asheville is known for its friendly, laid-back atmosphere and progressive spirit. Whether you're seeking outdoor adventure, cultural enrichment, or simply a peaceful mountain retreat, Asheville offers something for everyone, making it a truly unforgettable destination.

# For 30 Years, Warren Haynes' Christmas Jam Has Rocked Asheville — and Built Homes Along the Way

**ASHEVILLE, North Carolina** — On a cold December night in the mountains of western North Carolina, thousands of music fans pack into an arena, drawn by the promise of marathon sets, surprise guests, and the kind of loose, freewheeling collaborations that can only happen when great musicians share a stage with no rules and even fewer time limits.

But for guitarist Warren Haynes, the founder of the annual Warren Haynes Presents: Christmas Jam, the music has always been about something bigger than the notes.

"The whole idea was to give back to the community that raised me," Haynes said in an interview. "Asheville is my hometown. I grew up here. And when we realized we could use the music to actually build something real — to build homes for people who need them — it changed everything about what the Jam meant."

## From Humble Beginnings to a Marquee Event

What began in the late 1980s as an informal gathering of local musicians at a small Asheville club has grown into one of the most anticipated benefit concerts in American music. Over the decades, the Christmas Jam has hosted a staggering roster of talent — from members of the Allman Brothers Band and the Grateful Dead to Dave Matthews, Trey Anastasio, Gov't Mule, Branford Marsalis, and countless others.

Haynes, best known for his work with the Allman Brothers Band, the Dead, and his own band Gov't Mule, has long been the connective tissue of the American jam-band scene. That reputation has helped him attract musicians who show up not for a paycheck, but for the cause.

"Nobody's here to get paid," Haynes said. "Everybody donates their time. The musicians, the crew, everybody. That's what makes it special. When you take money out of the equation, people play differently. They play for each other."

## A Partnership Built to Last

For years, the Christmas Jam has partnered with Asheville Area Habitat for Humanity, funneling proceeds toward building affordable housing in the region. The collaboration has helped fund the construction of dozens of homes, transforming ticket sales and merchandise into foundations, framing, and front doors.

"Music is temporary — it happens in a moment and then it's gone," Haynes reflected. "But a house lasts. A family lives there for generations. That's a legacy you can touch."

Habitat organizers say the partnership has been transformative, not only for the funding it provides but for the visibility it brings to the region's affordable housing crisis.

"Warren could have chosen any charity in the world," said one longtime Habitat volunteer who has worked the event. "He chose to keep it local, to keep it here where people can see the results with their own eyes. When you drive through certain neighborhoods in Asheville, you're looking at homes that music built."

Many of the participating musicians have picked up hammers themselves, joining "build days" alongside volunteers in the days surrounding the concert.

## Musicians Answer the Call

For the artists who return year after year, the Jam has become a kind of family reunion — one with a purpose.

"There's nothing else like it," said one veteran guitarist who has played the event multiple times. "You get on that stage and you don't know who's going to walk out next to you. Warren might call up somebody you've idolized your whole life, and suddenly you're trading solos at two in the morning. And it's all going toward putting roofs over people's heads. How do you say no to that?"

That spirit of spontaneity is central to the Christmas Jam's identity. Sets routinely stretch past midnight, with rotating lineups and unrehearsed collaborations that give each year's show a one-of-a-kind character.

"You can't plan magic," Haynes said with a laugh. "You can only create the conditions for it and hope it shows up. And somehow, every year, it does."

## More Than a Concert

For Asheville, the Jam has become a point of civic pride — an annual reminder that a small mountain city can host something with national reach while keeping its heart firmly rooted at home.

As the event has grown, so has its ambition. Haynes has spoken often about wanting the model to inspire other musicians to leverage their platforms for community good.

"I hope people look at what we've done here and think, 'I could do that in my town,'" he said. "Every community has needs. Every musician has a stage. Put those two things together and you can change lives."

As another holiday season approaches and the amps are once again wheeled into place, Haynes says the mission remains as clear as it was on that first night decades ago.

"At the end of the day, we're just musicians trying to do a little good with the gift we've been given," he said. "If we can play some great music and build a few homes while we're at it — that's a pretty good night's work."

---

*The Warren Haynes Christmas Jam has raised millions of dollars for Habitat for Humanity and other charitable causes over the course of its decades-long run, cementing its place as one of the enduring institutions of American benefit concerts.*

# Local Musicians Unite for "Notes for Neighbors" Concert Benefiting Habitat for Humanity

**Charity event raises over $75,000 to fund construction of new homes for families in need**

By Staff Writer

A crowd of more than 1,200 people filled the Riverside Amphitheater on Saturday evening for "Notes for Neighbors," an annual charity concert that raised funds to support Habitat for Humanity's mission of building affordable housing for local families.

The sold-out event featured performances from a diverse lineup of regional and touring artists, all of whom donated their time and talent to the cause. Organizers announced that the concert generated more than $75,000 through ticket sales, merchandise, and a silent auction—enough to fund the construction of at least two new homes.

## Building Homes, One Song at a Time

"Every ticket sold tonight translates directly into lumber, nails, and hope for a family who has been dreaming of a place to call their own," said Maria Delgado, executive director of the local Habitat for Humanity chapter. "Music has this incredible power to bring people together, and tonight that power is building homes."

Habitat for Humanity, a nonprofit organization dedicated to eliminating substandard housing, relies on donations and volunteer labor to construct affordable homes. Partner families contribute "sweat equity" by helping build their own houses and later purchase them through affordable mortgage payments.

## Performers Share Their Motivations

For many of the artists, the cause struck a personal chord.

Singer-songwriter James Okonkwo, who headlined the event, spoke passionately about why he joined the lineup.

"I grew up in a household where housing stability wasn't guaranteed," Okonkwo said backstage. "When you know what it feels like to worry about where you'll live, you understand how life-changing a stable home can be. Playing this show isn't charity for me—it's a responsibility."

Folk duo The Hollow Pines, who opened the show, echoed similar sentiments.

"We've played a lot of gigs, but there's something different about looking out at the crowd and knowing that every person here is part of something bigger," said vocalist Rachel Simmons. "The energy is completely different when everyone shares a common purpose."

Local jazz artist Terrence Ward, a longtime supporter of the event, has performed at the concert for five consecutive years.

"I keep coming back because I've seen the results," Ward said. "I've visited the homes these concerts helped build. I've met the families. That's not an abstraction—those are real people with keys in their hands because a bunch of us decided to make some music."

## A Community Effort

Beyond the performances, the evening included testimonials from families who have benefited from Habitat's work. Among them was the Alvarez family, who moved into their Habitat-built home last spring.

"Before, we were renting a cramped apartment and never felt settled," said Carmen Alvarez, holding her young daughter. "Now my kids have their own rooms, a yard to play in, and a real sense of belonging. Events like this made that possible."

Volunteers staffed information booths throughout the venue, encouraging attendees to sign up for upcoming build days and ongoing donation programs.

## Looking Ahead

Organizers say they hope to expand the event next year, with plans to add a second night and invite additional performers.

"The response has been overwhelming," Delgado said. "This shows what's possible when a community comes together. We're already dreaming bigger for next year."

Those interested in supporting Habitat for Humanity's ongoing efforts can donate or volunteer through the organization's local chapter website.

*The next "Notes for Neighbors" concert is tentatively scheduled for the same time next year.*

# Musicians Strike a Chord for Community Amid Economic Downturn

*As the 2008 recession tightens its grip, artists turn their talents toward those who need it most*

As the financial crisis of 2008 continues to reshape the American economic landscape—wiping out savings, foreclosing homes, and leaving millions in uncertainty—an unexpected source of relief is emerging from concert stages across the country. Musicians, many of whom have their own reasons to worry about tour revenues and album sales in a contracting market, are increasingly using their platforms to give back to communities hit hard by the downturn.

Nowhere is this spirit more evident than in Asheville, North Carolina, where the annual Christmas Jam has become a shining example of how the music community can rally around a cause.

## A Mountain Town's Musical Tradition

Founded by acclaimed guitarist Warren Haynes—known for his work with the Allman Brothers Band and Gov't Mule—the Warren Haynes Christmas Jam has grown from humble local roots into a marquee event drawing top-tier talent to the Blue Ridge Mountains each December. What began as a gathering of friends jamming together has transformed into a benefit concert that channels the region's love of music into concrete community action.

The primary beneficiary of the event's fundraising efforts is Habitat for Humanity, the nonprofit organization dedicated to building affordable housing for families in need. In a year when housing has become the epicenter of economic anxiety—with foreclosure signs dotting neighborhoods nationwide—the partnership carries particular resonance.

## Music Meets Mission

"There's something powerful about musicians using their gifts to help people keep a roof over their heads," said one volunteer involved with the local Habitat chapter. "When so much of this crisis is about housing, it feels like the right fight at the right time."

The funds raised through ticket sales, auctions, and related events go directly toward Asheville Area Habitat for Humanity, helping to underwrite the construction of homes for local families. Over the years, the Christmas Jam has contributed to building numerous houses, providing not just shelter but stability for working families struggling to make ends meet.

For the musicians who participate—often donating their time and talent without compensation—the event represents a chance to reconnect with the fundamental purpose of their art. In an industry frequently criticized for excess, these benefit performances offer a counter-narrative: one of generosity and shared purpose.

## The Broader Movement

Asheville's Christmas Jam is part of a larger trend taking hold as the economy sours. Across genres and regions, artists are organizing benefit concerts, donating proceeds, and lending their names to causes ranging from food banks to unemployment relief funds. The recession has, paradoxically, sparked a renewed sense of civic engagement within the music world.

This impulse toward charity is not entirely new—musicians have long organized around causes, from Live Aid to Farm Aid—but the current economic emergency has given these efforts fresh urgency and local focus. Rather than distant global crises, many artists are now addressing hardship in their own backyards.

## Building Something That Lasts

What distinguishes the Habitat for Humanity model is its tangibility. Unlike donations that disappear into general funds, the outcome here is visible and permanent: a house, a home, a family with newfound security. In an era of economic abstraction—of collapsing markets and vanishing wealth measured in numbers most people never see—there is comfort in something as concrete as walls and a roof.

As the 2008 holiday season approaches under the shadow of recession, the Warren Haynes Christmas Jam stands as a reminder that community resilience often comes from unexpected places. When the music fades and the crowds disperse, what remains are homes built, families housed, and a demonstration that even in hard times, generosity can find a way to endure.

For a struggling nation, that may be the most valuable performance of all.

# From Garage Jams to Building Homes: How One Guitarist's Holiday Tradition Became a Movement

**A casual gathering of musician friends has transformed into an annual event that's helped construct dozens of affordable homes—proving that a little rhythm can build a lot of hope.**

---

When guitarist Marcus Reyes invited a handful of musician friends to his garage for an impromptu holiday jam session twelve years ago, he had modest ambitions: good music, cold drinks, and the warm company of people who shared his love for rock and roll.

"It was just us goofing around, playing the songs we grew up on," Reyes recalls, laughing as he tunes his weathered Fender in the same garage where it all began. "Somebody brought a cooler, somebody's cousin showed up with a bass. We had no idea we were starting anything."

But that first December gathering planted a seed that would grow into "Riffs for Roofs," now one of the region's most anticipated charity events, raising funds and awareness for affordable housing construction.

## An Unexpected Spark

The turning point came the following year, when a neighbor mentioned that a local family had lost their home. Reyes, moved by their story, suggested the group play a small public show and pass a hat for donations.

"We expected maybe fifty people and a couple hundred bucks," says longtime bandmate and drummer Denise Okafor. "Instead, the whole community showed up. We raised enough to help that family with a down payment. That's when Marcus got this look in his eye—the one that means trouble in the best possible way."

That "look" launched what would become an annual mission. Partnering with a local housing nonprofit, the informal jam session evolved into a full-scale benefit concert.

## Building Momentum—and Homes

Today, Riffs for Roofs draws thousands of attendees each holiday season, featuring dozens of local and touring musicians who donate their time and talent. Over the past decade, the event has raised more than $1.4 million, contributing to the construction of 27 affordable homes for families in need.

"Music brings people together in a way nothing else can," Reyes says. "We figured, why not channel that energy into something with a foundation—literally?"

The event has become a full-circle experience. Volunteers who received housing assistance now return to swing hammers on new builds, and several have taken the stage themselves.

Maria Delgado, whose family moved into one of the first homes funded by the event, now volunteers every year. "This isn't charity that makes you feel small," she says, wiping away tears. "Marcus and everyone here make you feel like family. They didn't just give us a house—they gave us a community."

## More Than Music

What sets the event apart, organizers say, is its grassroots spirit. There are no corporate headliners or lavish productions—just working musicians, dedicated volunteers, and a shared belief that everyone deserves a place to call home.

"People assume you need celebrities or huge budgets to make a difference," Okafor says. "But we've proven that ordinary people with a common purpose can move mountains—one chord at a time."

As Riffs for Roofs prepares for its milestone event this year, Reyes remains humble about his creation. Asked about his legacy, he pauses, running a hand along his guitar's neck.

"I'm just a guy who loves to play," he says softly. "But if a few power chords can help put a roof over someone's head, then I'll keep playing until my fingers fall off."

Then he grins, plugs in his amp, and lets the music—and the mission—ring on.
